what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Critical platform outages deserve independent, aviation-style public investigation
sections.para: On 5 October 2026 a GitHub Actions incident blocked deploys for two hours across every region, delaying this site's own release. Incidents at platforms this critical should be investigated independently, published with evidence and followed to the second and third stories. Encrypted vaults, read keys and agents now make that affordable.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: A global deploy outage is design, not bad luck
sections.para: From 19:11 UTC hosted runners stopped being reliably assigned, and the status page will only say delays and resolved. A fault reaching every customer reveals poor isolation. Aviation investigates independently and publishes; software stops at the first story, and the old cost objection has expired now evidence can live in encrypted vaults.

sections.label: What happened, as far as anyone outside can tell
sections.line: The status page understated a two-hour stop on deploys
sections.para: GitHub's updates ran from degraded performance at 19:11 to degraded availability at 20:47, with repository lists, billing and Pages hit later. Each word undersold it: no hosted-runner workflow could be relied on to start. My release, pushed at 19:23, was cancelled at 20:10 and went live two hours late after a fresh commit at 21:26.

sections.label: Why "everybody" is the point
sections.line: Hosted-runner failure for everyone signals missing isolation by design
sections.para: GitHub serves over 180 million developers and 71 million Actions jobs a day, and 59 percent of 805 surveyed organisations use one CI/CD tool. A fault reaching every customer in every region shows little isolation on the component that gates deploys. Buyers should also ask whether they can ship without their pipeline vendor.

sections.label: What aviation does instead
sections.line: Aviation became safe by investigating everything independently and publicly
sections.para: ICAO Annex 13 makes prevention the sole aim of independent investigation, with final reports within twelve months. The NTSB has issued over 15,500 tracked recommendations and publishes full dockets; NASA's ASRS has taken over two million confidential near-miss reports. Software has nothing similar, and the US Cyber Safety Review Board was disbanded in January 2025.

sections.label: Near misses, and counting the rolls of the dice
sections.line: Near misses reveal risk before damage, if counted
sections.para: Near misses deserve the same investigation as crashes, since only luck differs, and actual damage is often 10% or 1% of what was possible. Counting how often the same dice were rolled turns a one-off into a predictable event. GitHub knows how often runner assignment wobbled without reaching the status page; customers do not.

sections.label: The first, second and third story
sections.line: The third story, why fixes went unfunded, goes untold
sections.para: The first story is what happened, the second why the system allowed it, the third why the fix was not paid for. The 2023 UK air traffic failure got all three, with thirty-four recommendations closed by June 2026, while CrowdStrike's 2024 outage was investigated by the company itself. GitHub's third story is about hidden trade-offs.

sections.label: The what-if ladder
sections.line: Ninety minutes sits low on an unexamined what-if ladder
sections.para: What if GitHub were down for a day, a week, corrupted beyond restoring, or withdrawn by decision? Code survives in git but issues, reviews and pipelines may not, and no regulator has modelled a week without GitHub. Treating a global ninety-minute fault as minor means paying for the lesson later, at greater cost.

sections.label: Why the market does not fix this
sections.line: Customers cannot see resilience, so markets cannot price it
sections.para: GitHub may legitimately accept this level of resilience, but customers cannot see how close to the wind it flies. With high exit barriers, uptime becomes marketing and investment goes to features. Published independent investigation gives the engineers who know the single points of failure the evidence to win the business case.

sections.label: The objection, and why it has expired
sections.line: Vaults and read keys make incident investigation cheap now
sections.para: The old objection was that incident evidence is confidential, huge and costly to share. A provider can now capture logs and changes into a signed, versioned vault, give an investigator a read key to only what is needed, and let an agent do the first pass, with a derived vault per customer. Only the requirement is missing.

sections.label: What the regulation does and does not do
sections.line: DORA, NIS2 and SEC rules notify but never explain
sections.para: DORA designated nineteen critical ICT providers in November 2025 and the UK named four in July 2026; GitHub is not among them. NIS2 and SEC rules produce notifications, not published second stories. GitHub's monthly report gives one paragraph per incident, while trackers counted 257 incidents in the year to April 2026, a fifth in Actions.

sections.label: What I would ask for
sections.line: Four cheap asks: second stories, near misses, records, independence
sections.para: Critical platforms should publish the second story of every status-page incident within thirty days, report near misses in aggregate, capture evidence into signed versioned records by default, and have someone independent publicly review incidents that reach everyone. Customers should ask for the first now, and check their own second path to production.

sections.label: What is open
sections.line: The cause, second paths and costs remain unknown
sections.para: Still unknown: the incident's cause, how many organisations have a second path to production, and what a week without GitHub would cost. The incident vault exists only in pieces and has not been assembled for a real incident. This site's release got through on a retry; many will not have.

sections.line: Related articles: green builds, footprints, insiders and due diligence
sections.para: Links to Green does not mean live, Footprint and blast radius, The ultimate insider, Every risk is already accepted, and Send an agent, not a spreadsheet, the due diligence piece this incident delayed. sections.label: Sources
sections.line: Sources: GitHub status, aviation investigations, regulators and essays cited
sections.para: Sources include GitHub's status page and availability posts, and Dinis Cruz's briefs on near misses and second stories. Also ICAO Annex 13, NTSB reports on Alaska 1282 and the Washington collision, NASA ASRS, the NATS review, CrowdStrike's analysis, the Cyber Safety Review Board, DORA, NIS2, SEC rules and JetBrains' CI/CD survey.
